title: Rate of Reactions - Factors Affecting Reaction Speed
topic: Factors Affecting Rate of Reaction (Temperature, Pressure, Concentration, Surface Area)
subject: Chemistry

questions.question: A student measures how fast magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid at two different temperatures. Both experiments use the same mass of magnesium and same volume of acid.
options: The hotter mixture produces hydrogen gas faster and finishes sooner
The colder mixture produces hydrogen gas faster because particles are slower
Both mixtures produce gas at exactly the same rate regardless of temperature
The hotter mixture stops producing gas earlier than the cold one
questions.explanation: Higher temperature means particles have more kinetic energy → move faster → collide more frequently with greater force → more successful collisions per second → faster reaction rate.

questions.question: Magnesium powder reacts much faster with acid than equal mass of magnesium ribbon even though both contain same amount of metal. Why is this?
options: Powder has less total surface area exposed to reactants
Powder exposes more surface area allowing more collisions per second
Ribbon contains impurities that slow down the reaction
Powder dissolves completely which changes the reaction type
questions.explanation: Smaller particles = greater total surface area for same mass. More surface atoms exposed to acid molecules = more simultaneous collision opportunities = faster observed rate.

questions.question: When investigating one factor affecting reaction rate, why must you keep all other conditions identical between trials?
options: It makes the experiment easier to set up
Only then can you be sure which factor caused the difference in speed
Teachers prefer experiments that follow strict rules
More variable tests give more accurate equipment measurements
questions.explanation: Fair test principle: Changing only one variable at a time allows clear cause-effect relationship. If multiple factors change simultaneously, results become impossible to interpret properly.

questions.question: Graph comparison: Two experiments measure hydrogen gas collected over time using same mass zinc but different acid volumes. Curve A rises quickly and levels off first. Curve B rises slowly and reaches plateau later. Both plateaus at same height. What does the plateau height represent?
options: Maximum amount of product possible when limiting reactant used up
Total time taken for the reaction to complete
Average speed of all particles during the experiment
Concentration of the strongest acid solution used
questions.explanation: Plateau height shows maximum product formed when limiting reactant fully consumed. Different slopes mean different rates, but same starting materials mean same final yield possible.

questions.question: Student observes calcium carbonate reacting with acid. Powder form produces bubbles much faster than marble chips of equal mass. After both reactions complete, what can you expect about carbon dioxide produced?
options: Powder produces more CO₂ than chips because it reacted faster
Chips produce more CO₂ because they contained more mass
Both produce same volume of CO₂ if masses were equal
No CO₂ produced since calcium carbonate is insoluble
questions.explanation: Surface area affects SPEED not TOTAL PRODUCT. Same mass CaCO₃ means same theoretical yield regardless of how fast reaction proceeds to completion.

questions.question: Two gas-phase reactions studied at different pressures while keeping temperature constant. Experiment Q uses double the pressure of Experiment P. Which outcome correctly describes collision behavior?
options: Particles in Q move faster simply because pressure increased
Particles in Q collide more often because packed closer together
Pressure doesn't affect gas reaction speeds at all
Lower pressure causes spontaneous formation of new chemical bonds
questions.explanation: Higher pressure compresses gases into smaller space = more particles per unit volume = closer proximity = increased collision frequency = faster rate.

questions.question: A curve showing hydrogen volume versus time has steep initial slope then flattens toward horizontal line. What explains why the slope gets shallower as reaction continues?
options: Acid concentration decreases as reactants used up = fewer collisions per second
Temperature drops during reaction causing all particles to stop moving
Magnesium ribbon becomes smoother making it harder for acid to attack
Hydrogen gas produced blocks further acid contact with metal
questions.explanation: As reactants get consumed their concentration drops = fewer particles available per unit space = reduced collision frequency = slower rate observed by declining gradient.

questions.question: Which statement BEST summarises why increasing temperature accelerates most chemical reactions?
options: Particles gain energy needed to collide effectively more often
Molecular bonds weaken completely eliminating reaction barriers
Chemical identity changes at higher temperatures allowing new pathways
All collisions automatically become successful without any threshold
questions.explanation: Higher T increases average kinetic energy → larger fraction of collisions possess sufficient energy → more successful collisions per unit time = faster observed rate.

questions.question: Comparing two sets of experimental runs measuring oxygen produced from hydrogen peroxide decomposition: First set at room temperature completes in 6 minutes. Second set heated to 40°C completes in 1.5 minutes. Assuming same starting material amounts, what conclusion applies?
options: Higher temperature produced four times more oxygen gas
Higher temperature made reaction proceed four times faster
Room temperature experiment stopped prematurely due to error
Both experiments produced identical oxygen despite different completion times
questions.explanation: Completion time shorter at higher temperature indicates faster rate (6÷1.5=4 times faster). Same starting materials means same final oxygen yield regardless of path speed.

questions.question: For a valid scientific investigation comparing reaction rates, which experimental design correctly identifies and controls variables?
options: Change temperature AND concentration together to test real-world conditions
Keep all conditions constant except ONE factor you deliberately vary
Vary apparatus type randomly to check measurement reliability across tools
Change three variables simultaneously hoping one will show effect clearly
questions.explanation: Single-variable isolation ensures any observed difference in rate directly links to changed factor rather than confounding influences from other changing parameters.

questions.question:
In an experiment where sulfuric acid concentration affects copper sulfate crystal formation rate:

Trial X uses concentrated acid solution
Trial Y uses diluted acid solution
Both use same mass of copper oxide and same volume.

What observation would confirm Trial X has faster rate?
options: Trial X crystals form in shorter time period than Trial Y
Trial X produces more copper sulfate crystals overall
Trial Y crystals appear clearer than Trial X crystals
Both trials reach same endpoint at identical times
questions.explanation: Higher concentration provides more H₂SO₄ molecules per unit volume → more frequent collisions with CuO particles → faster reaction rate → shorter completion time. Final product amount depends on CuO mass.

questions.question: Why do fine wood shavings burn faster than thick wooden logs despite containing same total mass of wood?
options: Shavings have greater surface area allowing more oxygen collisions per second
Logs contain more water content slowing combustion significantly
Heat dissipates differently based on wood color variations
Air flow restrictions around large pieces prevent complete burning
questions.explanation: Greater surface area exposure allows simultaneous oxygen contact with more wood particles → increased collision frequency → faster burning rate without changing total combustible material available.

questions.question:
A student plots graphs showing methane gas volume produced over time from two different experimental setups:

Setup 1: High pressure container
Setup 2: Normal pressure container
Both use identical hydrogen and carbon reactants.

What graph feature distinguishes Setup 1 from Setup 2?
options: Setup 1 shows steeper rising curve reaching plateau faster
Setup 1 shows lower final plateau height indicating less methane
Setup 2 reaches plateau first due to better gas mixing
Both graphs overlap perfectly since pressure doesn't matter
questions.explanation: Higher pressure = gas particles packed closer = more frequent collisions between reactants = faster rate = steeper initial slope and earlier plateau achievement. Final yield stays same if reactant amounts identical.

questions.question:
During a lab experiment measuring hydrogen gas production from zinc reacting with acids:

Beaker A contains powdered zinc
Beaker B contains lumps of zinc
Equal volumes and concentrations of acid added to both.

What happens after BOTH reactions finish completely?
options: Both beakers contain equal hydrogen gas volume
Beaker A contains more hydrogen gas due to faster reaction
Beaker B contains more hydrogen gas due to slower heat loss
Neither reaction produces any measurable hydrogen
questions.explanation: Same zinc mass means same potential electron donation = same theoretical H₂ produced. Particle size affects rate not final quantity. Both reach identical gas volumes eventually if reaction completes fully.

questions.question:
A researcher compares reaction speeds for sodium thiosulphate plus hydrochloric acid at different temperatures. Results show:

Cold water bath: Cross disappears after 120 seconds
Warm water bath: Cross disappears after 45 seconds

What primary reason explains this difference?
options: Warm water provides more thermal energy for successful collisions
Cold water chemically reacts with thiosulphate reducing effective concentration
Time measurement errors occurred more frequently at low temperatures
Light visibility through cloudy solution differs based on container temperature
questions.explanation: Higher temperature increases molecular kinetic energy → more particles exceed minimum energy threshold → higher frequency of effective collisions → faster precipitation formation obscuring cross marker.

questions.question: Identify the scenario that demonstrates proper control of variables when testing concentration effect on reaction rate:
options: Using different masses of solid in each trial
Keeping temperature constant while varying only acid concentration
Changing both temperature and concentration simultaneously
Using different volumes of acid without controlling other factors
questions.explanation: Valid experiment isolates single independent variable. Temperature must remain constant while concentration varies systematically to establish clear relationship between these two factors alone.
